blocks: Person/Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande classified Hindustani ragas under ten parent scales, or thaats, in the early twentieth century, and named each after a prominent raga. Marwa is one of the ten.
A thaat is a classification. Ragas live inside it, each with its own phrases, ascent and descent, emphasized notes and performance time; a thaat itself is never performed.
The Carnatic system's equivalent parent scale is Gamanashrama, melakarta 53.
Raga Marwa, a sunset raga, omits Pa entirely and centers on komal Re and Dha.
Ragas Puriya and Sohini use the same notes with different emphasis: Puriya dwells in the lower register around Ni and Ga, and Sohini in the upper register around high Sa.
The thaat has both a raised fourth and a lowered second, so the tonic is approached by a half step from either side (N–S and r–S).

Hindustani pitches are tuned by ear against the tanpura drone and do not match equal temperament. The equal-tempered spelling on a Launchpad approximates the collection without its intonation or melodic rules.
On C: C D E♭ F G A♭ B. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 1 3 1. Music/Scale/Minor/Natural with a raised seventh.
The raised seventh came from cadential practice: musica ficta supplied a leading tone at cadences in modal polyphony long before any theorist listed the result as a scale.
"Harmonic minor" is a nineteenth-century pedagogical name. It collects the pitches of the chords of a minor key, with the dominant and leading-tone chords built on the raised seventh.
Common-practice harmony uses the collection for V, V7 and vii°7 in minor. Its melodies avoid the augmented second between ♭6 and 7, or fill it in, or turn it into a deliberate effect.
Nineteenth-century exoticism made that augmented second a marker of the East, Spain or Romani music.
Its fifth mode, C D♭ E F G A♭ B♭ on C, is Phrygian dominant. Flamenco, klezmer (where it is called Freygish or Ahava Rabbah) and Middle Eastern pop use it, and the maqam Hijaz is close to it.
The collection contains a fully diminished seventh chord (B D F A♭) and an augmented triad (E♭ G B). Those two symmetrical chords give it more harmonic ambiguity than the diatonic modes.

The MicroFreak manual lists its "Harmonic Minor" setting as C D E F G A♭ B. With E natural, that collection is harmonic major, Person/Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov's name for a major scale with a lowered sixth. The manual page is Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings; which collection the firmware plays is not documented there.
Also called Gypsy minor and double harmonic minor. On C: C D E♭ F♯ G A♭ B. Steps in semitones: 2 1 3 1 1 3 1. Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic with a raised fourth.

The name comes from the nineteenth-century style hongrois: the verbunkos idiom that Romani bands played in Hungarian cities, which Person/Franz Liszt, Person/Johannes Brahms and Person/Franz Schubert borrowed. Liszt's book on the subject, Des Bohémiens et de leur musique en Hongrie (18/5/9), credited that music to the Roma.

Person/Béla Bartók and Person/Zoltán Kodály's fieldwork after 1905 found that older Hungarian peasant song was largely pentatonic. The "Hungarian" in the scale's name therefore names an urban, Romani-performed popular style rather than Hungarian village song. See Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor.
Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsodies and the "alla zingarese" finales of Brahms and Person/Joseph Haydn draw on the idiom, usually as melodic color over functional harmony in harmonic minor.
Its two augmented seconds, ♭3–♯4 and ♭6–7, make it a quick shorthand for Eastern Europe in film and game scores.
It has two leading tones: F♯ leads to G and B leads to C. A melody can cadence on the dominant as strongly as on the tonic.
The step pattern 2 1 3 1 1 3 1 read backward is a rotation of itself, so the collection maps onto itself under inversion.
It is the fourth mode of the double harmonic major scale (C D♭ E F G A♭ B), which Arabic theory associates with maqam Hijaz Kar.

Also called jazz minor and, in its ascending form, the acoustic collection. On C, ascending: C D E♭ F G A B. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 2 2 1. The classical descending form is Music/Scale/Minor/Natural.

The classical form records voice leading. Raising both sixth and seventh on the way up avoids the augmented second of Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic while keeping the leading tone. Lowering both on the way down lets the line fall toward the dominant.
Baroque lines follow the harmony more than the direction. Over a dominant chord, Person/Johann Sebastian Bach's descending lines keep the raised sixth and seventh.

Twentieth-century jazz theory uses the ascending form in both directions and treats each of its modes as a chord-scale. Person/George Russell's Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization (1953) brought Lydian-based thinking into that theory.
Its modes cover much of jazz harmony beyond the diatonic system:
Mode 1, melodic minor on its own tonic, fits a minor-major seventh chord.
Its modes cover much of jazz harmony beyond the diatonic system:
Mode 3, Lydian augmented, fits a major seventh chord with a sharp fifth.
Its modes cover much of jazz harmony beyond the diatonic system:
Mode 4, Lydian dominant, fits a dominant seventh chord with a sharp eleventh, such as a tritone substitute.
Its modes cover much of jazz harmony beyond the diatonic system:
Mode 6, Locrian ♮2, fits a half-diminished chord.
Its modes cover much of jazz harmony beyond the diatonic system:
Mode 7, the altered scale or super Locrian, fits a dominant seventh chord with altered ninths and fifths.
Its modes cover much of jazz harmony beyond the diatonic system:
The fourth mode, C D E F♯ G A B♭ on C, approximates harmonics 8 through 14 of a fundamental on C. Writers on Person/Béla Bartók call it the acoustic or overtone scale for that reason.
The collection is one note away from both the major scale (lowered third) and Dorian (raised seventh).
Also called Aeolian and pure minor. On C: C D E♭ F G A♭ B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 1 2 2. The sixth mode of Music/Scale/Major.
Person/Heinrich Glarean named the mode on A Aeolian in the Dodecachordon (15/4/7). Before that, a D-final piece with a B♭ sounded the same collection while still counting as Dorian.

Common-practice minor was never this collection alone. Cadences raised the seventh, first through musica ficta and later in notation, and melodic lines raised or lowered the sixth as voice leading required. Natural, Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic and Music/Scale/Minor/Melodic are later pedagogical slices of one flexible minor mode.
Aeolian folk song keeps the minor dominant (v) and cadences without a leading tone.
Rock and film music use the Aeolian progressions i–♭VII–♭VI and i–♭VI–♭VII, which treat ♭VII as a dominant substitute. In C: Cm–B♭–A♭.
In jazz the Aeolian chord-scale fits a minor chord functioning as vi in a major key, where Dorian would put the raised sixth against the key.

The scale shares its key signature with its relative major. Baroque composers sometimes wrote minor pieces with one flat fewer than the modern signature, a holdover from Dorian notation; see Music/Scale/Dorian.
The ♭6 separates Aeolian from Dorian. Many melodies described as "minor" use only scale degrees 1 through 5 and never decide between them.

The MicroFreak's "Minor" setting is listed in its manual as C D E♭ F G A B♭ B, which lacks A♭, the note that separates natural minor from Dorian, and adds B natural. See Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings and Music/Scale/Dorian/Bebop. The Launchpad's "Natural Minor" setting carries this scale's name; its manual lists no pitches.
Also called the tetrardus authentic mode or Mode 7. On C: C D E F G A B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 2 1 2 2 1 2. The fifth mode of Music/Scale/Major.
The ancient Greek Mixolydian octave species ran from B to B, the collection now called Locrian. The medieval G mode inherited the name in the Carolingian renaming; see Music/Scale/Dorian.
In polyphony the G mode's seventh was routinely raised to F♯ at cadences, so much "Mixolydian" Renaissance music cadences as if in G major.

Folk traditions that end tunes without a leading tone favor it. Irish and Scottish dance tunes are often Mixolydian, and the Great Highland bagpipe chanter plays a Mixolydian scale on A with a flat seventh.
Rock uses its ♭VII as a third functional chord beside IV and V. The progression I–♭VII–IV–I closes "Hey Jude", and the Beatles' "Norwegian Wood" is Mixolydian throughout.
In jazz chord-scale theory it is the default scale over an unaltered dominant seventh chord.
The tonic triad is major, the triad on 5 is minor (G B♭ D on C), and the subtonic chord ♭VII is major. Cadences come from ♭VII–I or IV–I instead of V–I.
Inverting its step pattern gives Music/Scale/Minor/Natural.
Also called the Music/Anhemitonic pentatonic, gong mode in Chinese theory, and the MicroFreak's "Pentatonic" setting. On C: C D E G A. Steps in semitones: 2 2 3 2 3.

Five-note scales without semitones appear in traditions with no historical contact: Chinese, Korean, Japanese, West African, Andean, Scottish and Appalachian music among them. Chinese theory derived its five tones, gong shang jue zhi yu, from a chain of fifths by the third century BCE.

European art music took it up as a marker of the exotic or the rural. Person/Claude Debussy heard the Javanese gamelan at the 18/8/9 Exposition Universelle in Paris, and "Pagodes" (Estampes, 1903) is built on pentatonic collections. Javanese slendro tuning divides the octave into five near-equal steps, so the Western pentatonic is only an approximation of what he heard.
Folk melodies such as "Auld Lang Syne" and "Amazing Grace" are pentatonic.
Music education uses it for improvisation because it contains no semitones and no tritone. The Orff Schulwerk and Kodály methods start children on it.
Country, gospel and rock guitar use the major pentatonic for major-key soloing. Its five modes include Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor.
It is a stack of four perfect fifths (C G D A E).
The pitch-class complement of Music/Scale/Major is a pentatonic collection: the black keys of a piano form G♭ major pentatonic.
Also called la-pentatonic in Kodály solmization and yu mode in Chinese theory. On C: C E♭ F G B♭. Steps in semitones: 3 2 2 3 2. The fifth mode of Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major.

Person/Béla Bartók and Kodály's fieldwork after 1905 found that the oldest layer of Hungarian peasant song is in a minor pentatonic, often with a melody that repeats a fifth lower in its second half. Bartók set out that finding in The Hungarian Folk Song (1924). It overturned the nineteenth-century assumption that Hungarian music meant the style hongrois of Music/Scale/Minor/Hungarian.
The scale is also the foundation of blues and rock melody, where Music/Scale/Blues adds a ♭5 to it.
Rock and blues guitar organize improvisation around five fingerboard patterns of this scale, the "boxes".
Over a dominant seventh chord, the ♭3 grates against the chord's major third. Blues players treat that clash as the idiom.
Kodály pedagogy uses la-pentatonic for early minor-mode songs.
Every note of the scale is a chord tone or tension of a minor eleventh chord on the tonic (C E♭ G B♭ F), so the scale can be played over that chord with no avoid notes.
Also called the deuterus authentic mode or Mode 3. On C: C D♭ E♭ F G A♭ B♭. Steps in semitones: 1 2 2 2 1 2 2. The third mode of Music/Scale/Major.
The ancient Greek Phrygian octave species ran from D to D, the collection now called Dorian. The medieval name shifted with the rest of the Greek names; see Music/Scale/Dorian.

In chant and polyphony the E mode was hard to cadence in, because no leading tone rises to the final. Renaissance cadences in the E mode pair F–E in the bass with D–E above it. Heard from A minor, the result sounds like a half cadence.

That cadence outlived the mode. The Baroque "Phrygian half cadence", iv6–V in minor, uses the same half-step bass descent to the dominant. The two-chord Adagio of Person/Johann Sebastian Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 3 is one.
Flamenco's characteristic sound is usually Phrygian with a major tonic, close to the fifth mode of Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic, over the Andalusian cadence i–♭VII–♭VI–V.
Heavy metal leans on the ♭2 for darkness, often as a riff that alternates the tonic with ♭II.
In jazz chord-scale theory it fits a minor seventh chord functioning as iii, and the sus4♭9 chord voiced over it.
Carnatic music's Hanumatodi, melakarta 8, is this collection. See Music/Scale/Todi for the different Hindustani Todi.
It is the inversion of the major scale: the major step pattern read downward from the tonic gives Phrygian.
Phrygian and Locrian are the only diatonic modes with a ♭2. The ♭II triad sits a half step above a minor tonic, the relation the Neapolitan chord borrows in common-practice minor.
The tonic has no dominant: the triad on 5 is diminished (G B♭ D♭).
In sargam: S r g M' P d N. On C: C D♭ E♭ F♯ G A♭ B. Steps in semitones: 1 2 3 1 1 3 1.
One of Person/Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande's ten Hindustani thaats, named for raga Todi. See Music/Scale/Marwa for how a thaat relates to the ragas inside it.
The principal raga is Miyan ki Todi. Its name ties it to Miyan Tansen, the singer at Akbar's court in the sixteenth century.
The Carnatic equivalent parent scale is Shubhapantuvarali, melakarta 45.
Miyan ki Todi is a late-morning raga. Pa is weak or skipped in ascent, and the lowered Re, Ga and Dha are sung slightly flat of their equal-tempered pitches, with slow oscillation.
Gujari Todi drops Pa entirely; Bilaskhani Todi takes its notes from the Bhairavi thaat yet keeps the Todi name.
The name points to two different scales. Carnatic Todi, Hanumatodi or melakarta 8, has the notes of Music/Scale/Phrygian, while Hindustani Todi has a raised fourth and a raised seventh.
Its step pattern, 1 2 3 1 1 3 1, contains two augmented seconds, like Music/Scale/Minor/Hungarian, from which it differs only in the second degree.
Also Person/Olivier Messiaen's first mode of limited transposition. On C: C D E F♯ G♯ A♯. Steps in semitones: 2 2 2 2 2 2.
Glinka used a descending whole-tone scale for the sorcerer Chernomor in Ruslan and Lyudmila (18/4/2), and Russian composers after him kept it for the supernatural.
Person/Claude Debussy made it a harmonic field. "Voiles" (Préludes, Book I, 1909–1910) stays on one whole-tone collection for most of its length and turns pentatonic in the middle.
Messiaen listed it first among his modes of limited transposition in Technique de mon langage musical (1944), and said he avoided it because Debussy and Dukas had used it so thoroughly.
Impressionist harmony, and later film and television, use it for dreams, flashbacks and suspended time.
Jazz uses it over a dominant seventh chord with a ♯5 and 9 (C7♯5, C9♯5), and Person/Thelonious Monk made descending whole-tone runs a signature.

There are only two distinct whole-tone collections, the even and the odd pitch classes. Every rotation of the scale is the same scale, so it has no modes. On a device with root selection, the twelve roots produce only two sets of pitches.
It contains no perfect fifth, no leading tone and no minor or major triad; every triad built from it is augmented. No note can function as a tonic without help from outside the scale.
The French augmented sixth chord (A♭ C D F♯ in C) is a four-note subset of the scale, a pivot between functional and whole-tone harmony.

Standing supervision of the AI agents that do work in My/Knowledge/Garden/logseq-encode-garden. One chief-of-staff agent holds this graph's docket from a tmux session of its own, starts subagents for named work items, and reports outcomes, so names the work and reads results instead of driving each session. Its subagents and worktrees run in the harness's own subagents or in tmux; herdr is used only when asks for it.

A hayward kept the hedges and fences of the common fields, and kept the livestock out of the growing crop. The work here is the same shape: deciding what may be written into a public garden, keeping another repository's private context from crossing into it, and keeping links pointing at pages that exist.

The name belongs to the seat rather than to whichever session is sitting in it. A session ends, a model changes, an agent renames itself; the seat and its record carry on, and whoever takes it next inherits both. encode-garden-chief-of-staff describes a function and changes with the workspace label — Hayward does not.

The register is the one the other seats use, from Person/Steve Yegge/Agent: a reeve ran one estate, a seneschal ran the household above them, a hayward held the boundary. No agent on that roster carries this name.

Chiefs are conventionally named <workspace>-chief-of-staff, and the name is a hint rather than a mechanism. It is not how one is found. An agent can rename itself out of the convention and go on supervising, a chief with no pane carries no multiplexer name at all, and a name can be reassigned to a different session while staying valid — so matching on the suffix has no case left where it is sufficient. One filter run against the live set returned two of the chiefs that were working at that moment.

Find them by enumerating the registry by reference and taking each agent's role from its own report, or from the declaration kept in the repository it supervises. A repository saying who supervises it is a local declaration; it is not a cross-repository roster anyone has to maintain.

The name is not how one is reached either. Sending to a bare name reaches whichever session currently answers to it, which after a rename or reassignment is not the one meant. Address by name together with the listing's own reference, read fresh at the moment of sending rather than from memory. Absence from any listing means unknown, never that no chief is there.
Chiefs over other repos work from the declaration kept in their own repo.

The role's general shape travels with the agent from repo to repo. What a repo declares for itself is its docket, what counts as done, which subagents it starts, who commits, and which calls a chief settles alone. Those are the sections below.

This graph holds one such declaration. The other chiefs' declarations sit in their own repos, where this graph cannot read them, so the role lives here as a single page rather than as a type under Logseq/Entity with a definition page and instances. An agent arriving cold reaches it by the path My/AI/Agent/Chief of Staff and by the Chief of Staff title, which makes a rename here a decision for .
The page sits beside My/AI/Agent/Ask My Agent Anything About Me under My/AI/Agent/, which holds what this repo declares to an agent working in it.
Frontmatter is a [[Diataxis/How To]] tag, a see-also:: line reaching the garden page, herdr, and Logseq/Journal, and a github-link:: to the file on GitHub.
The daily record is nested underneath at My/AI/Agent/Chief of Staff/Log/YY/MM/DD Ddd, following Logseq/Best Practice/Utilize Date Namespacing Under Entity Name.
Standing upkeep of the graph: today's journal current, pages filed where the graph's conventions put them, links resolving, edits committed, and the workspace left in a state the human can walk into.
Work arrives as something to file — a page, a question, an import, a cleanup — or as a repair to something already here. A page written and left unlinked is the usual shape of unfinished work.
Opinions and principles that outlast one task belong here in the garden, under My/Pref or My/AI/Rule, where the agents in every repo can read them. Routing them here is part of the docket.

A work item is done when its links resolve against real pages and aliases, the day's journal carries the change, and the files are committed. The push waits for to ask for it in their own pane, and an unpushed stack earns no display line and no question — My/AI/Agent/Fleet.
Keeping journals/YYYY_MM_DD.md current is part of the job, and what the seat writes there is the / Updated change log — nothing else.

The narrative above the change log is 's, and the seat neither writes it nor removes it. Both halves matter: three agent-written narrative blocks were deleted from the 2026-08-18 Tue journal by hand, and a top-level block in codekiln's own voice was added above that day's hours later. Prose there is not evidence that anything went wrong.
Keeping journals/YYYY_MM_DD.md current is part of the job, and what the seat writes there is the / Updated change log — nothing else.

Logseq/Journal still instructs those blocks, and Logseq/Journal/Editorial headings exists to teach writing them. Following either reproduces the deletion — it has happened twice. Changing a convention page is codekiln's call, so the contradiction is carried on the seat's Heads Up Display rather than settled here.
Keeping journals/YYYY_MM_DD.md current is part of the job, and what the seat writes there is the / Updated change log — nothing else.
Work goes straight to main. The repo carries main plus the gh-pages branch the published site is built from, so a work item finishes without a feature branch or a review to wait on.
A graph has no build and no test suite, so the work left undone is the work nothing complains about. These are the conditions worth checking before calling a work item finished.

The check itself is the part that misleads. A line-based grep for those links reports breaks that are not there, because two link forms defeat it: a bare comment link may carry unencoded spaces in the page title, so a pattern that stops at whitespace truncates tmux/Keyshort/Pane/Resize Pane to tmux/Keyshort/Pane/Resize and reports it missing, and a URL assembled from adjacent string literals across two source lines exposes only its first fragment, so My/AI/Rule/ looks like a bare slash when the rest of the path is on the next line. Read the whole literal and decode before concluding a link is dead.

Two instruments have produced confident wrong answers here. File modification time reported .rulesync/ sources stale against the copies they generate, when the bodies matched exactly and the ordering was only checkout write order. A line-based pattern reported deep links dead when every target resolved, because it stopped at whitespace and read a truncated path as a target, and because it saw one URL's first fragment while the rest of the path sat on the next line.

scribe — standing for the day. Owns journals/YYYY_MM_DD.md and every commit. The other agents hand it finished files, and it writes the change log and commits them.
page-writer — one work item. Writes or rewrites pages, resolves its own links, and hands the file paths to the scribe.
harvester — reads a session that is finishing and files its conclusion as a page before the pane closes.
The agent name is <workspace-label>-<tab-label> inside 32 characters. This workspace's label is encode-garden, which leaves 18 characters for a tab label naming the work item.
A brief that stops at the page leaves the journal and the commit behind, so a brief written here names the scribe as the agent that commits.
